title: Australian MP Helen Haines leaves hospital after losing both legs in car attack
summary: Helen Haines, the Australian lawmaker who lost her legs after being repeatedly struck by a car in an attack, said on Monday she had been discharged from hospital and was now focused on rehabilitation.

image.caption: Australian MP Helen Haines, seen here in Parliament in October 2022, says she has been released from hospital. (AAP/Mick Tsikas/Reuters)

blocks.text: Helen Haines, the Australian lawmaker who lost her legs after being repeatedly struck by a car in an attack, said on Monday she had been discharged from hospital and was now focused on rehabilitation.
Haines, 65, was airlifted to hospital after being rammed outside her office

"This is a really positive moment," Haines said in her first public statement since being struck by an SUV on Oct. 19. She added that she appreciated the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages she had received from people throughout Australia and around the world.
"They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing."
Haines, 65, was airlifted to hospital after being rammed by a car outside her office in the small town of Wangaratta in the state of Victoria last month. Surgeons amputated both of her legs.

blocks.text: Brendan Nugent, a resident of the town ​of Tarrawingee within Haines's electorate, has been charged with three offences over the incident: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious ⁠injury, and causing harm to a public official.

During a court appearance in October, the accused's lawyer said his client had some mental health concerns and was also being treated for concussion, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation ​reported.

Haines, an independent lawmaker, was ​elected to Parliament in ⁠2019 for the rural seat of Indi, which she retained in 2022 and 2025.

Violent attacks on politicians are rare in Australia, where federal lawmakers, state leaders and even prime ministers are often seen shopping, grabbing coffee or attending community events with relatively little security.

However, concerns about politicians' safety have grown in ⁠recent years ​amid rising polarization, online abuse and threats against elected officials, prompting calls for ​greater protections while preserving the accessibility that has long characterized Australian politics.
